newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian-EC steel talks on new pact set for Feb 17.
newsitem.headline: Russian-EC steel talks on new pact set for Feb 17.

text.p: Russia and the European Commission will meet February 17 in Brussels to thrash out a steel export deal to replace an existing agreement due to expire in June, a trade official said on Monday.

"There are still many things which need to be decided, like how the negotiating process will be set up and what size of quotas will be involved," said the official, from the Foreign Economic Relations Ministry.
The first round of talks concluded in Moscow last week, but the official, who declined to be identified, said negotiations were still at an early stage.
"These were just preliminary talks, giving us the opportunity to discuss the issues," he said, adding that fundamental issues had not yet been addressed.

The two sides are hoping for a deal which will smooth the path towards a more open European market, on which Russian steel producers have come to depend more and more since domestic demand started to tumble early this decade.
The current agreement, originally covering 1995 and 1996, was extended by six months to give Russia and Europe time to negotiate a new pact.
It sets quotas on Russian steel exports to the European Union and to former East Germany at around 350,000 and 450,000 tonnes, respectively.
The EC has proposed extending the life of a new pact to five years and gradually opening the European market to more Russian steel.
"The EC's mandate is a gradual opening up of the market -- nothing too sudden," said an EC representative in Moscow.
The Commission also aims to have quotas which would discourage Russia from exporting steel cheaply, or dumping.
"The Russian steel industry should prepare itself for the opening of the European market so that it does not lead to swamping the market," the EC representative said.

Russia has proposed restructuring the make-up of quotas, allowing it to export more steel products for which there is strong demand while lowering quotas on products for which demand is low, Interfax reported last week.
Eurofer, a Brussels-based organisation representing the European iron and steel industry, said it wanted to link any increase in quotas to the rise in European steel demand.
"We propose that the evolution of quotas be similar to the evolution of real demand in the EC. This year we are forecasting a rise of two percent," said Elio Mauro, a Eurofer director.
The EC representative said he was hopeful for a new deal by the June deadline. "I am optimistic the talks will be completed by then," he said.
Russia produced 49.2 million tonnes of steel in 1996, down five percent from 1995 and only around half the peak levels reached in the late 1980s.
It exports around 60 percent of its steel output and domestic consumption is around 17 million tonnes annually, according to the International Iron and Steel Institute.
